subject: Business
title: Getting to Yes: The Final Agreement
description: A short lesson to help you apply Getting to Yes: The Final Agreement.

hook.text: You've been negotiating for weeks. Both sides are close. But nobody wants to make the last move.

buildup.text: Closing a deal requires someone to propose a specific, concrete package — not another counteroffer.

discovery.text: Summarize all agreed points, flag remaining gaps, and propose a resolution for each gap.

twist.text: Fear of commitment stalls many closings. Both sides worry they left money on the table.

climax.text: The 'single text' method: write one draft agreement and iterate on it together rather than trading offers.

punchline.text: Somebody has to say 'Here's the deal.' Be that person.

quiz.question: What is the 'single text' closing method?
options: Writing one draft agreement and iterating on it together
Sending a single email with your final offer
Only allowing one person to speak during closing

details.summary: Getting to yes requires moving from adversarial positions to collaborative problem-solving through Fisher and Ury's four principles: separate people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, generate options for mutual gain, and insist on objective criteria for evaluation.
details.whyItMatters: Getting to Yes transformed negotiation from intuition-based haggling into a principled methodology. Its framework for interest-based negotiation is taught in every major business school and used in diplomacy, business, and conflict resolution
takeaways: Separate people from the problem to keep negotiations productive and civil
Focus on underlying interests rather than stated positions to find solutions
Generate multiple options before evaluating any, then use objective criteria to decide

faq.question: What is the difference between positions and interests in negotiation?
faq.answer: A position is what someone says they want, like a specific salary number. An interest is why they want it, like financial security, recognition, or flexibility. Two people with incompatible positions may have compatible interests that creative solutions can satisfy simultaneously.

faq.question: How do you use objective criteria to break a negotiation deadlock?
faq.answer: Propose external standards both parties can agree are fair: market rates, industry benchmarks, precedents, expert valuations, or legal standards. Framing the discussion around what is fair by objective measures shifts focus from willpower to legitimacy and makes agreement easier.
